html:
Learning path

Track map

Start with how a model behaves. Add tools only after you can test a single call. Train only after the score says the cheaper fixes failed.

0 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 00 of 0
  1. 00

    Start here

    Learn how this course works, what to save as proof, and the safety rules that apply everywhere else.

    1. How to use this campus
    2. What you are learning to do
    3. Keep proof for every exercise
    4. Safety rules for every exercise
    5. What you need on your machine
    6. How the tracks fit together
  2. 01

    How models work

    Explain tokens, context, sampling, hallucination, and the model families named in current job posts.

    1. A model predicts the next token
    2. Tokens are the unit of cost and context
    3. The context window is one shared budget
    4. Temperature is a sampling control
    5. Hallucination is fluent text without evidence
    6. System, user, and tool messages do different jobs
    7. Model families you will see in 2026 job posts
    8. Choose a reasoning model or a fast chat model
    9. What a language model computes
    10. Transformers and attention, walked through
  3. 02

    Prompting

    Write prompts as jobs with a done-check, an output shape, and a test for the next change.

    1. Write the job, the input, and the done-check
    2. Lock the output shape
    3. Few-shot examples that do not leak
    4. Split a hard task into steps you can test
    5. Critique the draft, then revise once
    6. Prompt injection is untrusted text that pretends to be an order
    7. Change one thing, then score it
    8. Prompting and instruction design
    9. Structured outputs and tool calling
    10. Injection at the prompt boundary
  4. 03

    Local models

    Run an open-weight model on your own machine, pick a size that fits, and keep data separate from weights.

    1. Run a model locally when the data should stay put
    2. Install a runner and call it on localhost
    3. Pick a model size that fits in memory
    4. Quantization trades precision for fit
    5. Read the license before you ship a weight
    6. Keep a smoke test you can rerun
    7. Keep weights, prompts, and private data apart
  5. 04

    APIs and cost

    Call a hosted model without leaking the key, and read a bill in tokens, cache, and retries.

    1. Call an API without putting the key in the repo
    2. Ask for structured output and check it
    3. Set timeouts, retries, and a rate-limit plan
    4. Read the bill in tokens, cache, and batch
    5. Compare providers on the same ten tasks
    6. Log the call without logging the secret
    7. LLMOps in production
  6. 05

    Retrieval

    Build a retrieval pipeline that cites sources, and measure whether the right passage was found.

    1. Retrieve when the answer has to come from a source
    2. Chunk documents so a citation can point at them
    3. Search with keywords and with embeddings
    4. Rerank a short list before you prompt
    5. Cite a passage a person can open
    6. Failure modes to test before you tune the prompt
    7. Measure retrieval before you measure the answer
    8. RAG end to end
    9. Vector databases and hybrid search
  7. 06

    Agents

    Design a tool loop with a schema, a permission boundary, a step cap, and a trace.

    1. An agent is a loop with a stop rule
    2. Give every tool a name, a schema, and a handler
    3. Allow, deny, and ask a person
    4. Decide what the agent is allowed to remember
    5. Add another agent only when the handoff is a real artifact
    6. Read the trace, not the closing summary
    7. Make tool calls safe to retry, inside a sandbox
    8. Agents and the Model Context Protocol
    9. Multi-agent orchestration
  8. 07

    MCP

    Explain the Model Context Protocol and connect tools without granting a server silent access.

    1. MCP connects a model to tools you did not hard-code
    2. Host, client, and server have different jobs
    3. Tools act, resources are read, prompts are templates
    4. Connect a local server over stdio
    5. Consent, authentication, and untrusted servers
    6. How coding tools use MCP
  9. 08

    Coding agents

    Review an agent that edits a repository: plan, diff, tests, and a human gate.

    1. A coding agent edits a repository under rules
    2. Give the agent the files and tests that matter
    3. Plan, edit, run, then stop
    4. Review the diff and the tests
    5. Secrets, destructive git, and the network
    6. Use a coding agent on a team without shipping junk
  10. 09

    Evals

    Score quality, safety, latency, and cost on a versioned task set before you trust a change.

    1. An eval is a versioned test, not a feeling
    2. Start with ten tasks you can explain
    3. Score quality, safety, latency, and cost together
    4. Use a model as a judge only with a rubric and an audit
    5. Gate changes to the prompt, the model, and the index
    6. Put red-team cases in the set early
    7. Keep the scorecard next to the artifact
    8. Evals and observability
    9. Evals and guardrails in production
  11. 10

    Fine-tuning

    Decide when LoRA is the right next step, and compare an adapter to the base model on the same tasks.

    1. Fine-tune only after a measured failure of the cheaper fixes
    2. LoRA trains a small adapter and leaves the base model frozen
    3. Training data has a format, a license, and a leakage problem
    4. Compare the adapter to the base model on the same tasks
    5. Prefer a prompt or a tool when that is the whole gap
    6. Fine-tuning, LoRA, QLoRA, and distillation
  12. 11

    Safety

    Write a personal policy for data, tools, and the actions that always need a person.

    1. Write a one-page safety policy
    2. Decide retention before you log the prompt
    3. A person approves sends, payments, and deletes
    4. Write an incident note when the model misbehaves
    5. What this course will not help you do
    6. AI security and governance
  13. 12

    Product skills

    Specify an AI feature the way a product manager and an engineer can build and measure together.

    1. Name the job before you name the model
    2. Write a one-page spec
    3. Share four numbers with engineering
    4. Design the empty, slow, wrong, and unsafe states
    5. Ship a prototype, then an eval, then a limited release
    6. Add voice only when latency and handoff are designed
  14. 13

    Capstone

    Finish a small grounded assistant with citations, one tool, ten eval tasks, and a safety note.

    1. Choose a capstone you can finish on your own notes
    2. Write the acceptance tests before the prompt
    3. Keep a build log as you go
    4. Demo the capstone in ten minutes
    5. Decide the next change from the scorecard
  15. 14

    Contact center

    Place a voice model beside the queue, the recording, and the human who still owns the call.

    1. Contact center voice AI: the ASR, TTS, and LLM loop
    2. AI agents in the contact center
    3. AI in the contact center ecosystem
    4. Responsible AI and data privacy for voice
    5. Build a RAG voice agent for a contact center
  16. EX

    Ecosystem

    Map sister systems, ports, cutovers, and the claims this course will not certify.

    1. The ecosystem around a system you ship
    2. Architecture from a prompt to a gate
    3. Deployment and configuration walkthrough
    4. Migration and cutover from a legacy bot
    5. Troubleshooting playbook
    6. Ports, protocols, and a firewall study matrix
    7. Voice bridge: SIP, PSTN, recording, WFM, and emergency calls
    8. CRM, analytics, and API bridges
    9. AI agents beside a human queue
    10. Security, compliance, and the limits of this course
    11. Licensing, certification, and a career path
    12. Roadmap and what was not re-checked
